chapter.title: Storage and Retrieval
chapter.author: Martin Kleppmann
chapter.primary_goal: Understand how database storage engines lay out, index, update, compress, and retrieve data, and how OLTP and OLAP workloads lead to very different storage architectures.

chapter_summary.overview: Chapter 3 moves below the logical data models of Chapter 2 and examines how storage engines physically store and retrieve data. It begins with an append-only key-value log and derives the need for indexes, highlighting the fundamental tradeoff that indexes improve reads but add write overhead. Hash indexes such as Bitcask map keys to byte offsets and work well when keys fit in memory, while compaction, segment merging, tombstones, checksums, and recovery snapshots make append-only storage practical. SSTables add sorted keys, enabling sparse indexes, efficient range scans, compression, and merge-based compaction. A memtable plus SSTables forms the core of an LSM-tree, with an append-only recovery log protecting recent writes. Bloom filters and size-tiered or leveled compaction improve practical performance. B-trees take a different approach: fixed-size pages are updated in place, a root-to-leaf search provides logarithmic lookup, page splits keep the tree balanced, and a write-ahead log protects against crashes. The chapter compares B-trees and LSM-trees in terms of write amplification, sequential versus random I/O, read latency, compaction, fragmentation, and transactional semantics. It then surveys secondary, clustered, covering, multi-column, multidimensional, full-text, fuzzy, and in-memory indexes. The second half distinguishes OLTP from OLAP, motivates data warehouses and ETL, introduces star and snowflake schemas, and explains why column-oriented storage is effective for analytics. Column stores read only needed columns, compress repetitive values well, support bitmap and run-length encoding, improve CPU efficiency through vectorized processing, and can exploit sort order. Writes to column stores are often buffered and merged using LSM-like techniques. Finally, materialized views and data cubes precompute aggregates to accelerate common analytic queries at the cost of storage, write overhead, and reduced flexibility.
major_sections: Data Structures That Power Your Database

learning_objectives.objective: Explain why application developers benefit from understanding storage-engine internals.
Explain the append-only log example and why writes are fast but reads are O(n).
Define an index and explain the read/write tradeoff created by indexes.
Explain a hash index mapping keys to byte offsets and the Bitcask design.
Explain log segmentation, compaction, and segment merging.
Explain tombstones, crash recovery, checksums, and single-writer concurrency in append-only logs.
State the advantages and limitations of hash indexes.
Define SSTables and explain why sorted segments improve merging, indexing, compression, and range queries.
Explain memtables and the write/read/flush/compaction flow of SSTable storage.
Explain why a separate append-only log is used to recover the memtable after crashes.
Define LSM-trees and identify systems using LSM-style storage.
Explain Bloom filters and size-tiered versus leveled compaction.
Explain B-tree pages, root traversal, branching factor, and page splitting.
Explain B-tree crash recovery using a write-ahead log.
Explain B-tree concurrency control and optimizations such as copy-on-write and sibling pointers.
Compare B-tree and LSM-tree read/write characteristics.
Define write amplification and explain why it matters, especially on SSDs.
Explain how compaction can interfere with reads/writes and what happens if it falls behind.
Explain primary and secondary indexes and how nonunique secondary keys are represented.
Compare heap files, clustered indexes, and covering indexes.
Explain concatenated and multidimensional indexes.
Explain full-text/fuzzy indexing and Lucene's edit-distance approach.
Explain how in-memory databases achieve durability and why they can outperform disk-oriented designs.
Distinguish OLTP and OLAP access patterns.
Explain why organizations separate analytical workloads into a data warehouse.
Explain ETL.
Define fact tables, dimension tables, star schemas, and snowflake schemas.
Explain why wide fact tables motivate column-oriented storage.
Explain bitmap encoding, run-length encoding, and bitwise filtering.
Explain vectorized processing and CPU-cache efficiency in analytical databases.
Explain sort order in column stores and why multiple sort orders may help.
Explain how column stores handle writes using an in-memory sorted store and bulk merges.
Differentiate virtual views, materialized views, and data cubes.
Explain the chapter's top-level distinction between OLTP seek-bound workloads and OLAP bandwidth-bound workloads.

database_fundamentals: Retrieve that data later when requested.
storage_engine_foundations.why_internals_matter: Developers need enough understanding to choose a storage engine appropriate to the workload and tune it intelligently.
two_families_introduced: Page-oriented storage engines such as B-trees

simple_append_only_database.write: db_set appends key,value to the end of a file.
simple_append_only_database.read: db_get scans the file and returns the last occurrence of a key.
simple_append_only_database.read_problem: Lookup scans the entire file and is O(n).
simple_append_only_database.log_definition: An append-only sequence of records; not necessarily human-readable.

indexes.definition: Additional metadata derived from primary data that acts as a signpost for locating records.
indexes.multiple_indexes: Different query patterns may require different indexes.
indexes.write_tradeoff: Every index must be updated on writes, so indexes improve reads but slow writes.
indexes.design_rule: Choose indexes based on actual query patterns rather than indexing everything.

hash_indexes.structure: In-memory hash map: key -> byte offset in append-only data file.
hash_indexes.lookup: Hash lookup -> seek to byte offset -> read value.

bitcask_constraints.keys: All keys must fit in RAM.
bitcask_constraints.values: Values can exceed RAM because they remain on disk.

hash_indexes.good_workload: Many writes per key, but not too many distinct keys.
hash_indexes.segmenting: Close a segment at a size threshold and continue writes in a new segment.
hash_indexes.compaction: Discard obsolete duplicate values and retain only the newest value for each key.
hash_indexes.segment_merge: Merge several immutable compacted segments into a new segment in the background.
hash_indexes.read_across_segments: Check newest segment's hash map first, then older segment maps.

implementation_details.file_format: Binary length-prefixed records are preferable to CSV.
implementation_details.crash_recovery: Rebuild hash maps by scanning segments, or load saved hash-map snapshots.
implementation_details.concurrency: Often one writer thread; immutable segments allow concurrent readers.

append_only_advantages: Crash recovery and concurrency are simpler than in-place overwrite.
limitations: Hash table must fit in memory.

sstables_and_lsm_trees.sstable: Sorted String Table: each segment contains key-value pairs sorted by key, with one value per key within a merged segment.
advantages: Blocks can be compressed, reducing disk and I/O usage.
sstables_and_lsm_trees.merge_rule: If the same key appears in several input segments, keep the value from the most recent segment.
sstables_and_lsm_trees.sparse_index: Store offsets for only some keys. Sorting lets the engine jump near the desired key and scan a short range.
sstables_and_lsm_trees.memtable: In-memory balanced tree, such as a red-black or AVL tree, maintaining writes in sorted-key order.
write_flow: Append incoming write to the recovery log.
When memtable exceeds threshold, flush it as a sorted SSTable.
Continue writes in a new memtable.
read_flow: Continue through older SSTables if needed.
sstables_and_lsm_trees.recovery_log: Unsorted append-only log used only to reconstruct the memtable after a crash; discarded after flush.
sstables_and_lsm_trees.lsm_tree: Log-Structured Merge-Tree: storage design based on a cascade of sorted files merged and compacted in the background.
sstables_and_lsm_trees.related_search_engine: Lucene uses SSTable-like sorted files for term -> postings-list mappings.
sstables_and_lsm_trees.bloom_filter: Memory-efficient approximate-set structure that can tell when a key is definitely absent, avoiding unnecessary disk reads.

compaction_strategies.size_tiered: Merge newer/smaller SSTables into older/larger SSTables.
compaction_strategies.leveled: Split key ranges into smaller SSTables across levels; compaction is more incremental and can use less disk.

strengths: Works with data much larger than memory

b_trees.history: Introduced in 1970 and remains the standard index structure in many databases.
b_trees.organization: Fixed-size pages, traditionally 4 KB, read and written one page at a time.
structure: Interior pages defining key-range boundaries and child references
Leaf pages containing values or references to values
b_trees.branching_factor: Number of child-page references in a page; often several hundred.
b_trees.lookup: Start at root and follow range-appropriate child references until reaching a leaf.
b_trees.update: Find leaf page, modify it, and rewrite the page in place.
b_trees.insert: Add key to appropriate page; if full, split into two pages and update parent.
b_trees.balance: B-trees remain balanced with depth O(log n).
b_trees.chapter_example_capacity: A four-level B-tree with 4 KB pages and branching factor 500 can store up to 256 TB.

b_tree_reliability_and_optimizations.write_ahead_log: Append every modification to a WAL/redo log before modifying tree pages so crash recovery can restore consistency.
b_tree_reliability_and_optimizations.why_wal_needed: Operations such as page splits modify multiple pages; a crash midway can leave an inconsistent tree.
b_tree_reliability_and_optimizations.concurrency: Latches/lightweight locks protect B-tree structures during concurrent access.
optimizations: Abbreviated separator keys to increase branching factor.
Lay out nearby leaf ranges near each other on disk.
Sibling pointers between leaves for ordered scans.

rule_of_thumb.b_tree: Often thought faster/more predictable for reads.

b_tree_vs_lsm.benchmark_warning: Results depend heavily on workload and configuration; benchmark the actual workload.
b_tree_vs_lsm.write_amplification: One logical database write causes multiple physical disk writes over time.
b_tree_write_amplification: Potential extra writes from splits or double-write protection.
b_tree_vs_lsm.lsm_write_amplification: Repeated compaction and merging rewrites SSTable data.
why_lsm_can_write_faster: Often lower write amplification depending on configuration/workload.
Sequential SSTable writes instead of random page overwrites.
lsm_downsides: Reads may need to inspect several structures/segments.
Initial writes and compaction share finite disk bandwidth.
If compaction falls behind, segment count grows, disk may fill, and reads slow.
b_tree_vs_lsm.b_tree_transaction_advantage: Each key appears in exactly one place, making it convenient to attach range locks for strong transactional semantics.

representations: Key -> list of matching row IDs
Append row ID to the key to make index entries unique
secondary_indexes.engines: Can use either B-trees or log-structured indexes.

other_indexing_structures.heap_file: Unordered row storage separate from indexes. Secondary indexes point to row locations, avoiding full-row duplication.
other_indexing_structures.clustered_index: Stores the indexed row directly in the index; InnoDB's primary key is clustered.
other_indexing_structures.covering_index: Stores selected extra columns inside the index so some queries can be answered from the index alone.
other_indexing_structures.tradeoff: Clustered/covering indexes improve reads but consume more storage and add write/consistency overhead.

multi_column_and_specialized_indexes.concatenated_index: Combines several fields into one ordered key, e.g. (lastname, firstname). Useful for leading-prefix queries.
multi_column_and_specialized_indexes.leading_prefix_limitation: An index on (lastname, firstname) supports lastname and lastname+firstname, but not firstname alone.
multi_column_and_specialized_indexes.multidimensional_indexes: Needed when several independent dimensions must be constrained simultaneously, such as latitude/longitude.
approaches: Map dimensions to one value using a space-filling curve and use a normal B-tree.
Use specialized spatial structures such as R-trees.
multi_column_and_specialized_indexes.full_text_and_fuzzy: Require techniques beyond exact/range indexes; full-text engines can use linguistic analysis and edit distance.
multi_column_and_specialized_indexes.lucene: Uses SSTable-like term files plus an in-memory finite-state automaton/trie-like index; Levenshtein automata support edit-distance search.

in_memory_databases.why_disk_is_hard: Disk storage requires careful layout; disks are durable and historically cheaper per GB than RAM.
in_memory_databases.restart: Reload state from disk or another replica.
in_memory_databases.why_still_in_memory: Reads are served from memory; disk may only be used as an append-only durability log.
in_memory_databases.counterintuitive_speed_reason: The performance advantage is not simply avoiding disk reads; OS caches may already prevent disk reads. In-memory systems avoid encoding in-memory structures into disk-oriented layouts.
in_memory_databases.model_advantage: Can implement structures such as priority queues and sets more naturally.
in_memory_databases.anti_caching: Evict least-recently-used records to disk and bring them back when needed, similar to virtual memory but at record granularity.

oltp.main_read_pattern: Small number of records per query, fetched by key.
oltp.main_write_pattern: Random-access, low-latency writes from user input.

oltp_vs_olap.transaction_note: In this context transaction processing means low-latency reads/writes; it does not necessarily imply ACID.

data_warehousing.reason: Ad hoc analytic scans can be expensive enough to harm latency and availability of business-critical OLTP systems.
data_warehousing.warehouse: Separate database containing a mostly read-only analytical copy of data from many OLTP systems.

etl.extract: Read data from OLTP systems or update streams.
etl.transform: Clean and reshape data into an analysis-friendly schema.
etl.load: Write transformed data into the warehouse.

data_warehousing.benefit: Warehouse can use a storage engine optimized specifically for analytics.
data_warehousing.sql_interface_note: OLTP DBs and warehouses may both expose SQL even though their internals differ dramatically.

star_and_snowflake_schemas.star_schema: Fact table at the center surrounded by dimension tables, visually forming a star.
star_and_snowflake_schemas.fact_table: Very large event table; each row represents an event such as a purchase, page view, or click.
star_and_snowflake_schemas.fact_attributes: Measurements such as quantity, sale price, cost, etc.
star_and_snowflake_schemas.dimension_tables: Describe who, what, where, when, how, and why of each event.
star_and_snowflake_schemas.snowflake_schema: More normalized variation where dimensions are decomposed into subdimensions.
star_and_snowflake_schemas.why_star_often_preferred: Simpler for analysts to work with.

column_oriented_storage.problem: Analytic fact tables may have trillions of rows and hundreds of columns, while a query often reads only a few columns.
column_oriented_storage.row_oriented: Stores all values for one row together.
column_oriented_storage.column_oriented: Stores all values of each column together, preserving row order across column files.
column_oriented_storage.benefit: Queries read/parse only needed columns, reducing disk I/O.
column_oriented_storage.nonrelational_example: Parquet supports a document model using columnar storage.

column_compression.why_effective: Values within a column are often repetitive.
column_compression.bitmap_encoding: For n distinct values, maintain n bitmaps; bit k indicates whether row k contains that value.
column_compression.run_length_encoding: Compress long runs of zeros/ones in sparse/repetitive bitmaps.

query_examples.AND: Bitwise AND bitmaps from multiple predicates.

vectorized_processing.idea: Operate on chunks of compressed column data in tight loops that fit in CPU cache and exploit SIMD instructions.
benefits: More values fit in L1 cache.
Bitwise operations can work directly on compressed chunks.

sort_order_in_column_storage.rule: Columns cannot be sorted independently; all columns must preserve corresponding row positions.
sort_order_in_column_storage.primary_sort_key: Choose based on common filters, e.g. date_key for date-range queries.
sort_order_in_column_storage.secondary_sort_key: Break ties in the first key, e.g. product_sk within date.
sort_order_in_column_storage.compression_benefit: Sorting creates longer runs of repeated values, improving run-length compression.
sort_order_in_column_storage.multiple_sort_orders: Replicated copies can be stored in different sort orders so queries use the copy best matching their access pattern.
sort_order_in_column_storage.analogy: Multiple sort orders resemble multiple secondary indexes, but replicas contain full values rather than pointers.

writing_to_column_stores.problem: Compressed sorted columns are difficult to update in place.
solution: Buffer writes in an in-memory sorted structure.
Periodically merge accumulated writes with on-disk column files.
writing_to_column_stores.query_behavior: Queries combine on-disk column data with recent in-memory writes; optimizer hides this distinction.

materialized_views_and_cubes.virtual_view: Stored query definition; query expands and executes underlying logic at read time.
materialized_views_and_cubes.materialized_view: Actual persisted copy of query results.
materialized_views_and_cubes.materialized_view_tradeoff: Speeds reads but underlying changes require updating the copied results, increasing write cost.
materialized_views_and_cubes.data_cube: Materialized grid/hypercube of aggregates grouped by multiple dimensions.
materialized_views_and_cubes.benefit: Common aggregate queries can be answered from precomputed totals.
materialized_views_and_cubes.limitation: Cannot answer dimensions/conditions that were not represented in the cube.
materialized_views_and_cubes.best_practice: Keep raw data and use cubes/aggregates as targeted performance accelerators.

flashcards.front: What are the two fundamental jobs of a database?
flashcards.back: Store data and retrieve it later.

flashcards.front: Why should application developers care about storage-engine internals?
flashcards.back: To choose and tune an engine appropriate to their workload.

flashcards.front: What two storage-engine families are introduced?
flashcards.back: Log-structured storage engines and page-oriented engines such as B-trees.

flashcards.front: What does db_set do in the simple example?
flashcards.back: Appends a key-value pair to a file.

flashcards.front: What does db_get do?
flashcards.back: Scans for the key and returns its most recent value.

flashcards.front: Why is the simple write fast?
flashcards.back: Appending to a file is efficient.

flashcards.front: What is a log in this book?
flashcards.back: An append-only sequence of records.

flashcards.front: What is the lookup complexity of the simple db_get?
flashcards.back: O(n).

flashcards.front: What is an index?
flashcards.back: Additional metadata derived from primary data that helps locate records.

flashcards.front: What is the fundamental index tradeoff?
flashcards.back: Faster reads but slower writes because the index must also be maintained.

flashcards.front: Why don't databases index everything by default?
flashcards.back: Indexes add storage and write overhead; they should match query patterns.

flashcards.front: What does a simple hash index map?
flashcards.back: Key -> byte offset in the data file.

flashcards.front: What engine is cited as using this idea?
flashcards.back: Bitcask.

flashcards.front: What must fit in RAM for Bitcask?
flashcards.back: All keys/hash-map entries.

flashcards.front: Can Bitcask values exceed RAM?
flashcards.back: Yes, because values stay on disk.

flashcards.front: What workload suits Bitcask?
flashcards.back: Many writes per key with relatively few distinct keys.

flashcards.front: Why split a log into segments?
flashcards.back: To bound file size and enable compaction/merging.

flashcards.front: What is compaction?
flashcards.back: Discard duplicate old values and keep only the most recent value per key.

flashcards.front: Can compaction/merge happen in the background?
flashcards.back: Yes, while old segments still serve reads/writes.

flashcards.front: How are reads performed across multiple hash-indexed segments?
flashcards.back: Check newest segment first, then progressively older ones.

flashcards.front: What record marks deletion in an append-only log?
flashcards.back: A tombstone.

flashcards.front: How can hash maps be recovered after restart?
flashcards.back: Scan segments or load stored hash-map snapshots.

flashcards.front: How are partially written log records detected?
flashcards.back: Checksums.

flashcards.front: What writer concurrency pattern is common for sequential append logs?
flashcards.back: One writer thread.

flashcards.front: Why can many readers access immutable segments safely?
flashcards.back: Segments are append-only and then immutable.

flashcards.front: Why are append-only writes attractive?
flashcards.back: They are sequential, simplify crash recovery/concurrency, and avoid fragmentation via merging.

flashcards.front: What is a key limitation of hash indexes?
flashcards.back: The hash table must fit in memory.

flashcards.front: Why are range queries poor with hash indexes?
flashcards.back: Keys are not maintained in sorted order.

flashcards.front: What does SSTable stand for?
flashcards.back: Sorted String Table.

flashcards.front: What ordering does an SSTable require?
flashcards.back: Key-value pairs are sorted by key.

flashcards.front: How many times should a key appear in a merged SSTable segment?
flashcards.back: Once.

flashcards.front: Why is SSTable merging efficient?
flashcards.back: Sorted inputs can be merged like mergesort.

flashcards.front: If a key appears in several segments, which value survives?
flashcards.back: The value from the most recent segment.

flashcards.front: Why can an SSTable use a sparse in-memory index?
flashcards.back: Sorting lets the engine seek near the key and scan a short region.

flashcards.front: What does SSTable block compression save?
flashcards.back: Disk space and I/O bandwidth.

flashcards.front: What is a memtable?
flashcards.back: An in-memory sorted tree holding recent writes.

flashcards.front: Name common memtable structures.
flashcards.back: Red-black tree or AVL tree.

flashcards.front: When is a memtable flushed?
flashcards.back: When it grows past a size threshold.

flashcards.front: What is a memtable flushed as?
flashcards.back: An SSTable.

flashcards.front: What is the LSM read order?
flashcards.back: Memtable, newest SSTable, then older SSTables.

flashcards.front: Why keep a separate append-only log in an LSM engine?
flashcards.back: To recover recent memtable writes after a crash.

flashcards.front: When can the recovery log be discarded?
flashcards.back: After the corresponding memtable is flushed to SSTable.

flashcards.front: What does LSM stand for?
flashcards.back: Log-Structured Merge-Tree.

flashcards.front: Name LSM-style systems from the chapter.
flashcards.back: LevelDB, RocksDB, Cassandra, HBase.

flashcards.front: How does Lucene use an SSTable-like idea?
flashcards.back: Term -> postings-list mappings are stored in sorted segment files.

flashcards.front: What problem do Bloom filters optimize?
flashcards.back: Negative lookups for keys that do not exist.

flashcards.front: What can a Bloom filter tell you reliably?
flashcards.back: That a key is definitely not present.

flashcards.front: What is size-tiered compaction?
flashcards.back: Merge newer/smaller SSTables into older/larger SSTables.

flashcards.front: What is leveled compaction?
flashcards.back: Organize smaller SSTables into levels/key ranges for incremental compaction.

flashcards.front: Why are LSM trees good for range queries?
flashcards.back: Data is stored sorted by key.

flashcards.front: Why are LSM trees good for writes?
flashcards.back: Disk writes are largely sequential.

flashcards.front: What is the most widely used index structure?
flashcards.back: The B-tree.

flashcards.front: How are B-trees physically organized?
flashcards.back: Fixed-size pages, traditionally around 4 KB.

flashcards.front: What page starts a B-tree lookup?
flashcards.back: The root page.

flashcards.front: What does an interior B-tree page contain?
flashcards.back: Key-range boundaries and references to child pages.

flashcards.front: What is a B-tree branching factor?
flashcards.back: Number of child-page references in a page.

flashcards.front: Typical B-tree branching factor?
flashcards.back: Often several hundred.

flashcards.front: How is an existing B-tree key updated?
flashcards.back: Find the leaf page, modify it, rewrite the page.

flashcards.front: What happens when a B-tree page is full during insert?
flashcards.back: Split it into two pages and update the parent.

flashcards.front: What is B-tree depth complexity?
flashcards.back: O(log n).

flashcards.front: What capacity example is given for a 4-level B-tree?
flashcards.back: Up to 256 TB with 4 KB pages and branching factor 500.

flashcards.front: What is a B-tree WAL?
flashcards.back: Write-ahead/redo log written before page updates.

flashcards.front: Why is the WAL necessary?
flashcards.back: A crash during a multi-page update could otherwise corrupt the tree.

flashcards.front: What protects B-tree structures during concurrent access?
flashcards.back: Latches/lightweight locks.

flashcards.front: What is copy-on-write in B-trees?
flashcards.back: Write modified pages elsewhere and update parent references rather than overwriting.

flashcards.front: Why abbreviate separator keys?
flashcards.back: Fit more keys per page and increase branching factor.

flashcards.front: Why add sibling pointers to leaf pages?
flashcards.back: Efficient ordered scans without returning to parents.

flashcards.front: Rule of thumb: which is faster for writes, LSM or B-tree?
flashcards.back: LSM-tree.

flashcards.front: Rule of thumb: which is often faster/more predictable for reads?
flashcards.back: B-tree.

flashcards.front: Why must this rule of thumb be treated cautiously?
flashcards.back: Benchmarks depend on workload and configuration.

flashcards.front: What is write amplification?
flashcards.back: One logical write causes multiple physical writes over time.

flashcards.front: Why is write amplification important on SSDs?
flashcards.back: Flash blocks have limited overwrite endurance and disk bandwidth is finite.

flashcards.front: Why can LSMs have higher write throughput?
flashcards.back: Sequential SSTable writes and often lower write amplification/fragmentation.

flashcards.front: Why can LSM storage be smaller?
flashcards.back: Better compression and less page fragmentation.

flashcards.front: What can compaction do to tail latency?
flashcards.back: Cause high-percentile latency spikes.

flashcards.front: What if compaction can't keep up?
flashcards.back: Segments accumulate, disk may fill, and reads slow down.

flashcards.front: Why must LSM compaction be monitored?
flashcards.back: Some engines don't automatically throttle incoming writes when compaction falls behind.

flashcards.front: What B-tree property helps transaction locking?
flashcards.back: Each key exists in one place in the index.

flashcards.front: What is a primary-key index used for?
flashcards.back: Uniquely locating a row/document/vertex.

flashcards.front: What is a secondary index?
flashcards.back: Index on non-primary attributes; keys need not be unique.

flashcards.front: How can a secondary index represent duplicate keys?
flashcards.back: Map key to a list of row IDs or append row ID to make entries unique.

flashcards.front: What is a heap file?
flashcards.back: Unordered row storage referenced by indexes.

flashcards.front: Why use a heap file with multiple indexes?
flashcards.back: Keep actual row data in one place and let indexes point to it.

flashcards.front: What is a clustered index?
flashcards.back: An index that stores the actual row with the indexed key.

flashcards.front: What is InnoDB's clustered index?
flashcards.back: The table's primary key.

flashcards.front: What is a covering index?
flashcards.back: An index containing selected extra columns so a query can be answered from the index alone.

flashcards.front: Tradeoff of clustered/covering indexes?
flashcards.back: Faster reads but more storage, write overhead, and consistency work.

flashcards.front: What is a concatenated index?
flashcards.back: A multi-column index built by concatenating fields in a fixed order.

flashcards.front: What is the leading-prefix limitation?
flashcards.back: (lastname, firstname) helps lastname queries but not firstname-only queries.

flashcards.front: Why are multidimensional indexes needed?
flashcards.back: To constrain several dimensions simultaneously, such as latitude and longitude.

flashcards.front: Name a spatial indexing structure.
flashcards.back: R-tree.

flashcards.front: What is a space-filling-curve strategy?
flashcards.back: Map multidimensional coordinates to one number and index it with a B-tree.

flashcards.front: Why are fuzzy indexes different?
flashcards.back: They search similar values, not just exact or ordered ranges.

flashcards.front: What edit distance means one letter inserted/deleted/replaced?
flashcards.back: Edit distance 1.

flashcards.front: What does Lucene use in memory for term lookup?
flashcards.back: A finite-state automaton similar to a trie.

flashcards.front: What automaton supports edit-distance search?
flashcards.back: Levenshtein automaton.

flashcards.front: Why have in-memory databases become practical?
flashcards.back: RAM has become cheaper and many datasets fit in memory.

flashcards.front: How can an in-memory DB achieve durability?
flashcards.back: Battery-backed RAM, disk log, snapshots, or replication.

flashcards.front: Why is a DB still 'in-memory' if it writes a disk log?
flashcards.back: Reads use memory; disk is only for durability/recovery.

flashcards.front: Name in-memory DB examples.
flashcards.back: VoltDB, MemSQL, Oracle TimesTen, RAMCloud, Redis, Couchbase.

flashcards.front: Why can in-memory DBs be faster even when disk DB blocks are cached?
flashcards.back: They avoid disk-oriented encoding/layout overhead.

flashcards.front: What is anti-caching?
flashcards.back: Evict cold records to disk and reload them when accessed.

flashcards.front: What does OLTP stand for?
flashcards.back: Online Transaction Processing.

flashcards.front: What is OLTP's read pattern?
flashcards.back: Small number of records fetched by key.

flashcards.front: What is OLTP's write pattern?
flashcards.back: Random-access low-latency user-driven writes.

flashcards.front: What does OLAP stand for?
flashcards.back: Online Analytic Processing.

flashcards.front: What is OLAP's read pattern?
flashcards.back: Large scans and aggregates over many records.

flashcards.front: What is OLAP's write pattern?
flashcards.back: Bulk import/ETL or event streams.

flashcards.front: What does OLTP data usually represent?
flashcards.back: Latest/current state.

flashcards.front: What does OLAP data usually represent?
flashcards.back: Historical events.

flashcards.front: Typical OLTP dataset size?
flashcards.back: Gigabytes to terabytes.

flashcards.front: Typical OLAP dataset size?
flashcards.back: Terabytes to petabytes.

flashcards.front: Why separate analytics from OLTP?
flashcards.back: Large scans can harm latency and availability of transaction workloads.

flashcards.front: What is a data warehouse?
flashcards.back: Separate database containing analytical copies of data from OLTP systems.

flashcards.front: What does ETL stand for?
flashcards.back: Extract-Transform-Load.

flashcards.front: What does ETL transform data into?
flashcards.back: An analysis-friendly, cleaned schema.

flashcards.front: Why can a warehouse use different storage internals despite also using SQL?
flashcards.back: Its workload is analytical rather than transactional.

flashcards.front: What is a star schema?
flashcards.back: Fact table in the center with surrounding dimension tables.

flashcards.front: What does a fact-table row represent?
flashcards.back: An event such as a sale, page view, or click.

flashcards.front: What do dimensions describe?
flashcards.back: Who, what, where, when, how, and why of an event.

flashcards.front: Why can dates be dimensions?
flashcards.back: They can encode holidays and other date metadata.

flashcards.front: What is a snowflake schema?
flashcards.back: A more normalized star-schema variant with subdimension tables.

flashcards.front: Why are star schemas often preferred?
flashcards.back: They are simpler for analysts.

flashcards.front: Why are fact tables challenging?
flashcards.back: They may contain trillions of rows and hundreds of columns.

flashcards.front: How many fact-table columns does a typical analytic query often read?
flashcards.back: Only around 4–5.

flashcards.front: What is row-oriented storage?
flashcards.back: Store all values from one row together.

flashcards.front: What is column-oriented storage?
flashcards.back: Store all values from each column together.

flashcards.front: Why is columnar storage efficient for analytics?
flashcards.back: Queries read only the columns they need.

flashcards.front: What nonrelational columnar format is named?
flashcards.back: Parquet.

flashcards.front: What invariant lets a column store reconstruct rows?
flashcards.back: Each column stores rows in the same order.

flashcards.front: Why does column storage compress well?
flashcards.back: Values within a column are often repetitive.

flashcards.front: What is bitmap encoding?
flashcards.back: One bitmap per distinct value, with one bit per row.

flashcards.front: How do you query value A OR B using bitmaps?
flashcards.back: Bitwise OR the corresponding bitmaps.

flashcards.front: How do you query condition A AND B?
flashcards.back: Bitwise AND the corresponding bitmaps.

flashcards.front: What can compress sparse bitmaps?
flashcards.back: Run-length encoding.

flashcards.front: Are Bigtable/Cassandra/HBase column families truly column-oriented in this sense?
flashcards.back: No; rows within a family are still stored together.

flashcards.front: What is vectorized processing?
flashcards.back: Process compressed column chunks in tight CPU-efficient loops, often using SIMD.

flashcards.front: Why does compression help CPU efficiency?
flashcards.back: More values fit into CPU cache.

flashcards.front: Can column files be sorted independently?
flashcards.back: No; row correspondence would be lost.

flashcards.front: Why sort by date_key first?
flashcards.back: Date-range queries can scan only the relevant rows.

flashcards.front: How can sorting improve compression?
flashcards.back: Repeated values form long runs suitable for run-length encoding.

flashcards.front: Why store replicated column data in different sort orders?
flashcards.back: Different query patterns benefit from different orderings.

flashcards.front: Why are column-store writes hard?
flashcards.back: Sorted compressed columns cannot be efficiently updated in place.

flashcards.front: How are writes commonly handled?
flashcards.back: Buffer in memory, sort, then bulk-merge with on-disk columns.

flashcards.front: What is a virtual view?
flashcards.back: A stored query definition evaluated when read.

flashcards.front: What is a materialized view?
flashcards.back: A persisted copy of query results.

flashcards.front: Why do materialized views make writes more expensive?
flashcards.back: Underlying changes must update the copied result.

flashcards.front: What is a data cube?
flashcards.back: A materialized multidimensional grid of aggregates.

flashcards.front: What is a cube's main benefit?
flashcards.back: Common aggregates become very fast because they are precomputed.

flashcards.front: What is a cube's limitation?
flashcards.back: It cannot answer arbitrary conditions/dimensions not represented in the cube.

flashcards.front: What is OLTP often bottlenecked by?
flashcards.back: Disk seek time.

flashcards.front: What is OLAP often bottlenecked by?
flashcards.back: Disk bandwidth.

scenario_questions.scenario: A key-value database receives millions of writes but has only a few hundred thousand distinct keys.
scenario_questions.question: What early chapter design fits well?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: An append-only log with an in-memory hash index, similar to Bitcask, because keys fit in memory and values can remain on disk.

scenario_questions.scenario: An append-only database keeps growing because the same keys are updated repeatedly.
scenario_questions.question: How does the chapter reclaim space?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Split into segments, compact each segment to keep newest values, and merge immutable segments in the background.

scenario_questions.scenario: A delete must survive future segment merging.
scenario_questions.question: What record is needed?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: A tombstone indicating that older values for the key must be discarded.

scenario_questions.scenario: A key does not exist in an LSM database, causing checks of many SSTables.
scenario_questions.question: What optimization helps?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: A Bloom filter can quickly indicate that the key is definitely absent and avoid unnecessary disk reads.

scenario_questions.scenario: A B-tree page split updates two child pages and a parent, then the machine crashes halfway through.
scenario_questions.question: What mechanism protects recovery?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Write the modification first to the write-ahead/redo log so the tree can be restored to a consistent state.

scenario_questions.scenario: An SSD-backed write-heavy database is wearing flash and saturating disk bandwidth.
scenario_questions.question: Which metric/tradeoff should you inspect?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Write amplification: how many physical writes the storage engine performs per logical write.

scenario_questions.scenario: An LSM database works well initially but later disk fills and reads get slower as writes continue.
scenario_questions.question: What might be happening?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Compaction may be unable to keep up, causing unmerged segments to accumulate and consume disk/bandwidth.

scenario_questions.scenario: A table has several secondary indexes and you want only one physical copy of each row.
scenario_questions.question: What layout helps?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Store rows in a heap file and let secondary indexes point to heap locations.

scenario_questions.scenario: A frequent query needs only indexed columns plus one extra attribute.
scenario_questions.question: What index can avoid a heap lookup?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: A covering index including that extra column.

scenario_questions.scenario: You have an index on (lastname, firstname) but frequently search by firstname only.
scenario_questions.question: Why is the index ineffective?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Concatenated indexes primarily support leading prefixes; firstname is not the leading field.

scenario_questions.scenario: A restaurant app queries bounding boxes over latitude and longitude.
scenario_questions.question: What type of index is appropriate?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: A multidimensional spatial index such as an R-tree, or a space-filling curve mapped to a one-dimensional index.

scenario_questions.scenario: Users expect misspelled product names to return close matches.
scenario_questions.question: Why won't a normal B-tree/LSM range index be enough?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Fuzzy matching requires similarity/edit-distance techniques such as Lucene's Levenshtein automata.

scenario_questions.scenario: A business analyst runs a huge full-table aggregate against the same DB serving checkout traffic.
scenario_questions.question: What architecture does the chapter recommend?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Move analytics to a separate data warehouse populated from OLTP data, preventing analytic scans from harming transactional latency.

scenario_questions.scenario: A sales warehouse has one event table linked to product, store, date, customer, and promotion tables.
scenario_questions.question: What schema pattern is this?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: A star schema with a central fact table and dimension tables.

scenario_questions.scenario: A fact table has 150 columns, but a query reads only date, product, and quantity across billions of rows.
scenario_questions.question: What storage layout is advantageous?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Column-oriented storage because it reads only the required columns instead of entire rows.

scenario_questions.scenario: A product column has 100,000 distinct product IDs over billions of rows and queries often use IN lists.
scenario_questions.question: What compression/filter structure is useful?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Bitmap encoding, potentially run-length compressed, allowing IN predicates to be evaluated with bitwise OR.

scenario_questions.scenario: An analytic engine is no longer disk-bound but spends time moving/decompressing values through CPU cache.
scenario_questions.question: What technique is relevant?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Vectorized processing over compressed column chunks, exploiting cache locality and SIMD.

scenario_questions.scenario: Most warehouse queries filter by date, then group by product.
scenario_questions.question: What sort order makes sense?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: date_key first, product_sk second, matching common filtering/grouping patterns.

scenario_questions.scenario: A column store receives continuous writes but on-disk data is sorted and compressed.
scenario_questions.question: How can it accept writes efficiently?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Buffer recent writes in an in-memory sorted structure and periodically bulk-merge them with on-disk column files, LSM-style.

scenario_questions.scenario: Analysts repeatedly ask for daily sales totals by store.
scenario_questions.question: What can accelerate this and what is the tradeoff?
scenario_questions.expected_answer: A materialized view/data cube can precompute totals, making reads fast but increasing write/storage cost and reducing flexibility.

short_answer_questions.question: Why are indexes a tradeoff rather than a free optimization?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: They add derived structures that speed reads, but every write must also update those structures, consuming storage and write I/O.

short_answer_questions.question: How does Bitcask turn an append-only file into an efficient key-value store?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: It keeps an in-memory hash map from each key to the byte offset of its newest value, while values stay on disk.

short_answer_questions.question: Why are immutable segments useful?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: They simplify concurrent reads and crash recovery; background compaction can build new merged segments and atomically replace old ones.

short_answer_questions.question: What does sorting buy you in SSTables?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Efficient merges, sparse indexes, range scans, and block compression because nearby key ranges are physically grouped.

short_answer_questions.question: Walk through an LSM-tree write and read.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Writes append to a recovery log and update a sorted memtable; full memtables flush to SSTables and are compacted. Reads check memtable, newest SSTable, then older SSTables.

short_answer_questions.question: How does a B-tree differ fundamentally from an LSM-tree?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: B-trees update fixed-size pages in place and use a WAL for recovery; LSMs append/flush sorted segments and merge them in the background.

short_answer_questions.question: What is write amplification and how do the two major designs incur it?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: A logical write results in multiple disk writes. B-trees write WAL plus pages and sometimes splits/double writes; LSMs rewrite data during repeated compactions.

short_answer_questions.question: Why can compaction become an operational problem?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Compaction consumes finite disk bandwidth, can increase tail latency, and if it falls behind, segments and disk usage grow while reads slow.

short_answer_questions.question: Compare heap, clustered, and covering index layouts.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Heap files store rows separately and indexes point to them; clustered indexes place full rows in the index; covering indexes place selected extra columns in the index.

short_answer_questions.question: Why aren't ordinary one-dimensional indexes enough for geospatial bounding boxes?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Latitude and longitude must be constrained simultaneously. A one-dimensional sorted index efficiently restricts one dimension at a time, so multidimensional structures such as R-trees are useful.

short_answer_questions.question: What is surprising about in-memory database performance?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Their advantage is not simply avoiding disk reads, because OS caches may already do that. They can avoid the overhead of disk-oriented encoding and data structures.

short_answer_questions.question: What is the central OLTP versus OLAP distinction?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: OLTP handles many low-latency point queries and user writes over current state; OLAP handles fewer but much larger scans/aggregations over historical data.

short_answer_questions.question: Why is a data warehouse separate from OLTP systems?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Expensive ad hoc analytics can scan large datasets and degrade production transaction performance, while a warehouse can be optimized for analytical access.

short_answer_questions.question: Explain fact and dimension tables.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Facts are high-volume event rows with measurements and foreign keys; dimensions provide descriptive context such as product, date, store, promotion, and customer.

short_answer_questions.question: Why is column-oriented storage well suited to analytics?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Analytic queries scan many rows but usually need only a few columns. Column stores read only those attributes and compress homogeneous values efficiently.

short_answer_questions.question: How do bitmap indexes evaluate filters?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Each distinct value has a bitmap. OR combines alternative values such as IN lists; AND combines predicates across columns.

short_answer_questions.question: What is vectorized processing?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Analytic operators process compact chunks of column values in tight loops that fit CPU cache and exploit SIMD, reducing branches and per-row function overhead.

short_answer_questions.question: Why can sort order improve both queries and compression in column stores?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Queries can scan only relevant key ranges, and repeated values become long runs that compress well.

short_answer_questions.question: How does an analytical column store solve its write problem?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Use an LSM-like in-memory buffer for recent writes, then merge those writes with immutable/compressed on-disk column files in bulk.

short_answer_questions.question: Compare virtual views, materialized views, and data cubes.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Virtual views are stored query definitions; materialized views persist results; data cubes are multidimensional materialized aggregates optimized for repeated analytical summaries.

common_confusions.confusion: An index is part of the primary data and has no write cost.
common_confusions.correction: An index is a derived structure. It speeds selected reads but must be updated on writes.

common_confusions.confusion: Append-only means data can never be deleted.
common_confusions.correction: Deletions are represented by tombstones, and old data is removed during compaction.

common_confusions.confusion: SSTables require an in-memory entry for every key.
common_confusions.correction: Because keys are sorted, a sparse index is enough; the engine can scan a short range.

common_confusions.confusion: An LSM recovery log must be sorted.
common_confusions.correction: It does not need sorting because its only job is to reconstruct the memtable after a crash.

common_confusions.confusion: Bloom filters prove a key is present.
common_confusions.correction: Their key benefit here is efficiently determining that a key is definitely absent; positive results may need verification.

common_confusions.confusion: B-trees and LSM-trees use the same physical update model.
common_confusions.correction: B-trees overwrite fixed pages in place; LSM designs append/flush immutable sorted files and compact them.
Performance depends on workload/configuration; the chapter explicitly recommends empirical testing.

common_confusions.confusion: Write amplification is only an LSM problem.
common_confusions.correction: Both B-trees and LSMs cause multiple physical writes per logical write, for different reasons.

common_confusions.confusion: Column-family databases such as Cassandra are the same as analytic column stores.
common_confusions.correction: The chapter says their column families still store a row's columns together and are mostly row-oriented.

common_confusions.confusion: A transaction-processing database must provide ACID merely because it is OLTP.
common_confusions.correction: Here transaction processing means low-latency reads/writes; ACID is a separate topic.

common_confusions.confusion: OLAP and OLTP can use the same engine equally well because both speak SQL.
common_confusions.correction: Their access patterns and bottlenecks differ enough that internals often diverge significantly.

common_confusions.confusion: Column stores are faster because they never scan many rows.
common_confusions.correction: They may scan millions/billions of rows, but read only needed columns and encode them compactly.

common_confusions.confusion: Each column in a column store may be sorted independently.
common_confusions.correction: Row positions must correspond across all columns, so the entire row order must be consistent.

common_confusions.confusion: Materialized views are just query shortcuts.
common_confusions.correction: Virtual views are query shortcuts; materialized views physically store query results.

common_confusions.confusion: Data cubes replace the need to retain raw data.
common_confusions.correction: Cubes accelerate predefined dimensions but are less flexible, so warehouses generally retain raw data.

practice_problems.prompt: A log has 10 million records and no index. What happens to lookup cost when it grows to 20 million records?
practice_problems.solution: With O(n) scan-based lookup, lookup work roughly doubles.

practice_problems.prompt: A hash index says key X is at byte offset 25,000. What does the engine do?
practice_problems.solution: Seek directly to that byte offset in the data file and read the value.

practice_problems.prompt: A segment contains k=1, k=2, k=3. What remains after compaction?
A key is missing from memtable and newest SSTable. What happens next?
practice_problems.solution: Check progressively older SSTables; Bloom filters can help skip files that definitely do not contain the key.

practice_problems.prompt: A B-tree insert fills a leaf page. What structural changes occur?
practice_problems.solution: Split the page into two and update the parent with the new key-range subdivision.

practice_problems.prompt: A logical write causes WAL write, page write, and an extra split-related write. How many physical write events are involved in this simplified example?
practice_problems.solution: At least three physical write events; this illustrates write amplification.

practice_problems.prompt: You have a concatenated index (country, city). Which query is naturally supported: country='US' or city='Atlanta' only?
practice_problems.solution: country='US' is naturally supported because country is the leading field.

practice_problems.prompt: Classify: 'Fetch account 123 and update balance' versus 'Compute average monthly balance across 50 million accounts.'
practice_problems.solution: First is OLTP; second is OLAP.

practice_problems.prompt: Rows matching product=A are 10110 and rows matching store=X are 11010. What bitmap represents A AND X?
A dashboard repeatedly shows yesterday's sales by store. What optimization could help?
practice_problems.solution: A materialized aggregate/data cube storing sales totals by date and store.

must_memorize: Indexes speed reads but add write overhead.
Append-only logs make writes simple and fast.
Hash index = key -> byte offset; Bitcask requires keys to fit in RAM.
Segments + compaction + merging reclaim log space.
Tombstones represent deletion; checksums detect partial records.
Hash indexes are poor for range queries.
SSTable = sorted immutable key/value segment.
Sorted segments enable sparse indexes, merges, range scans, and compression.
LSM path = WAL -> memtable -> SSTable -> compaction.
Bloom filters accelerate negative lookups.
Compaction strategies include size-tiered and leveled.
B-tree = fixed-size pages, root-to-leaf lookup, balanced O(log n), page splitting.
B-trees use WAL/redo logs for crash recovery and latches for concurrency.
LSMs usually favor write throughput; B-trees often favor read predictability.
Write amplification affects both B-trees and LSMs.
Compaction can create tail latency and must keep up with ingestion.
Secondary indexes may contain duplicate keys.
Heap file = one row copy plus index pointers.
Clustered index stores full rows; covering index stores selected extra columns.
Concatenated indexes obey leading-prefix behavior.
R-trees support multidimensional/geospatial indexing.
Lucene supports fuzzy matching using edit-distance techniques.
In-memory DB durability can come from logs, snapshots, or replication.
OLTP = many low-latency point reads/writes over current state.
OLAP = fewer but massive scans/aggregations over history.
OLTP is often seek-bound; OLAP is often disk-bandwidth-bound.
Data warehouse isolates analytical scans from OLTP.
ETL = Extract-Transform-Load.
Star schema = central fact table + dimensions.
Snowflake schema further normalizes dimensions.
Column storage reads only needed attributes.
Bitmap + run-length encoding compress repetitive column values.
OR combines alternatives; AND combines predicates.
Vectorized processing uses compressed column chunks and CPU/SIMD efficiently.
Column stores preserve the same row order across columns.
Sorting helps query pruning and compression.
Column-store writes can use LSM-like memory buffers and bulk merges.
Materialized views persist query results.
Data cubes precompute multidimensional aggregates but sacrifice flexibility.
final_review.memory_chain: APPEND LOG -> INDEX TRADEOFF -> HASH INDEX -> SEGMENTS/COMPACTION -> SSTABLE -> MEMTABLE -> LSM -> BLOOM FILTER -> B-TREE -> WAL -> LSM vs B-TREE -> SECONDARY/CLUSTERED/COVERING -> MULTIDIMENSIONAL/FUZZY -> IN-MEMORY -> OLTP vs OLAP -> WAREHOUSE/ETL -> STAR/SNOWFLAKE -> COLUMN STORE -> BITMAP/RLE -> VECTORIZED PROCESSING -> SORT ORDER -> BULK MERGE WRITES -> MATERIALIZED VIEW -> DATA CUBE
final_review.one_sentence_takeaway: Storage-engine design is a sequence of workload-specific tradeoffs: OLTP relies on indexes and structures such as B-trees or LSM-trees to make point reads/writes efficient, while OLAP relies on compact columnar layouts, compression, sequential scans, and precomputed aggregates to maximize analytical throughput.
